title: The 2,000-year-old perfume
whisper: kyphi, a recipe carved in stone
renderedWith: raea/sillage-002-kyphi (map fields unused; this file holds the script and the voice)

beats.say: This perfume is over {2,000|two thousand} years old. You cannot buy it. But its recipe is carved into a temple wall.
Egypt. The temple of Edfu, built more than {2,000|two thousand} years ago. Its priests call this perfume kyphi.
In one room, the walls list the recipes, step by step. Scholars call it the laboratory.
A Greek writer, Plutarch, says they burned incense three times a day: frankincense at dawn, myrrh at noon, and kyphi at dusk.
His recipe has {16|sixteen} ingredients. Honey. Wine. Raisins. Myrrh. Resin. Juniper berries. Even bitumen.
It is mixed while sacred texts are read aloud to the perfumers. And it is not only burned: it is also a drink, and a balm.
But here is the problem. Nobody agrees on the list.
One ancient doctor, Dioscorides, counts ten ingredients. Galen, fifteen. A later recipe, thirty-six.
And some of the Egyptian plant names? Scholars still cannot say what they were.
So anyone who makes kyphi today is reconstructing it, one guess at a time.
The recipe survived more than {2,000|two thousand} years. The exact smell did not.
All we really have is the wall.
